analogy.p: Imagine the nucleus as a **pea** placed at the centre spot of a football pitch, with the edge of the atom at the far boundary of the stadium. The pea is only about 1 cm across and the pitch is about 100 m wide, which is a ratio of about 1 to 10 000, just like the nucleus compared with the atom. A ball fired at the pitch would nearly always go through the empty space and only very rarely hit the pea, like the alpha particles. The analogy breaks down because the 'empty space' in an atom is not truly empty (electrons move through it) and a real nucleus is far denser than a pea, holding almost all the mass.
analogy.t: A pea in a football stadium

bullets: An **element** contains only one sort of atom, for example oxygen, O2, contains only oxygen atoms.
A **compound** contains two or more different elements **chemically combined** in fixed proportions, for example CO2 or NaCl.
Atoms are far too small to see with a light microscope, so our knowledge comes from **indirect evidence** from experiments.
Chemical symbols have a capital first letter, and a lower-case second letter if there is one (Co is cobalt, CO is carbon monoxide).
Everything in this topic links to the **periodic table**, which is arranged by atomic number.
A **model** is not 'wrong' because it is later replaced: each model explained the evidence available at the time.
core.p: All substances are made of **atoms**. An atom is the **smallest part of an element that can exist**, and each element is made of just one type of atom. There are about 100 different elements, each with its own symbol (for example C, Na, Cl) listed in the **periodic table**. When atoms of two or more elements are chemically joined, they make a **compound**; compounds can only be separated by chemical reactions, while mixtures can be separated by physical methods. The model of the atom is a **scientific model**: a simplified idea that explains the evidence we have, and it has changed as better evidence arrived.

bullets: The model of the atom changed in this order: **Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford (nuclear), Bohr, then the discovery of the neutron by Chadwick**.
A model is judged by whether its **predictions agree with experimental results**; a model that fails a test must be modified or replaced.
New models often keep the good parts of the old one, for example Bohr kept Rutherford's nucleus and added shells.
Ideas are checked by **other scientists repeating the work** (peer review), so the new model becomes accepted over time.
Be able to say **why** a model was replaced: it could not explain a specific observation.
The timeline is not just dates: the examiners reward the link 'result, therefore conclusion'.
core.h: 2. How and why scientific models change
core.p: A scientific model is accepted because it explains **all the evidence known at the time**. When a new experiment produces results that the current model cannot explain, scientists propose a **new or adapted model** which does explain them, and this is then tested by further experiments. This is why the atom model has changed several times, and it is a favourite exam theme: you must always link **new experimental evidence** to **the change in the model**. The key point is that evidence comes first, and the model is changed to fit it, not the other way round.

bullets: Atoms were thought of as like **tiny snooker balls**: solid, indivisible and with no parts inside.
Different elements were thought to have different sized/massed atoms.
Dalton's model did **not** contain electrons, protons or neutrons.
It could not explain **electricity** (why charges can be moved on or off atoms) or why substances conduct.
It was replaced when electrons were discovered, because an indivisible sphere cannot contain smaller particles.
The word **atom** comes from a Greek word meaning 'cannot be cut', which fits Dalton's idea.
core.p: At the start of the 19th century, **John Dalton** described atoms as **tiny, solid spheres that could not be divided**. In his picture, each element was made of its own type of sphere, and compounds formed when different spheres joined. This model explained the known **laws of chemical combination**, for example why elements combine in fixed proportions. It was a good model because it matched the evidence of the time, but it had no idea about internal structure or electric charge.

bullets: Evidence: electrons discovered, so the atom must have **smaller parts** and Dalton's indivisible sphere was wrong.
Plum pudding = **ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded**; the total charge is zero.
The positive charge was **spread out evenly**; there was no separate nucleus.
The model correctly said that atoms contain negative electrons and are neutral overall.
It predicted that fast positive particles fired at the atom would pass through with only **very small deflections**; the next experiment proved this wrong.
Exam tip: describe the plum pudding model in terms of **charge** (positive ball, negative electrons), not just 'a pudding'.
core.h: 4. Thomson: the discovery of the electron and the plum pudding model (1897)
core.p: In 1897 **J. J. Thomson** did experiments with electric currents in gases at low pressure (cathode rays) and found that they were made of particles much **smaller than the atom** and carrying **negative charge**. These were the **electrons**, which proved that atoms are **not indivisible**. Since atoms are neutral overall, Thomson proposed the **plum pudding model**: the atom is a **ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it**, like plums or raisins in a pudding. The positive charge was spread throughout the whole ball, and the charges balanced so that the atom is neutral.

bullets: Apparatus: a source of **alpha particles**, a **thin gold foil**, and a detecting screen that can be moved around the foil.
Gold was used because it can be hammered into an **extremely thin foil**, only a few atoms thick.
Observation 1: **most alpha particles passed straight through** the foil undeflected.
Observation 2: **some were deflected** through small angles.
Observation 3: **a very small number (about 1 in several thousand) were deflected back** through angles larger than 90 degrees, bouncing back towards the source.
The experiment is done in a **vacuum** so air molecules do not absorb or scatter the alpha particles.
core.h: 5. The alpha particle scattering experiment (Geiger and Marsden, 1909)
core.p: Under the direction of **Ernest Rutherford**, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired a beam of **alpha particles** at a very **thin sheet of gold foil** and detected where the particles went using a fluorescent (zinc sulfide) screen that flashes when hit. Alpha particles are **positively charged** (they are helium nuclei), so they are strongly affected by other positive charges. If the plum pudding model were correct, the spread-out positive charge should only deflect the alpha particles by a tiny amount. The results were completely different, and this is one of the most important experiments in science.

bullets: Straight through, therefore **mostly empty space**.
Deflected (small angle), therefore the nucleus is **positively charged** (like charges repel).
Bounced back (rare), therefore the nucleus is **very small, very dense and contains most of the mass**.
Only a few bounce back, therefore the nucleus is **very small compared to the atom** (few particles are on a direct collision course).
Plum pudding would predict **no large deflections at all**, so it was rejected.
Mark scheme language: 'a small number of alpha particles were deflected through large angles' means the positive charge is **concentrated in a small region**.
core.h: 6. Explaining the results: why the plum pudding model failed
core.p: Each observation must be matched with its conclusion, and this is exactly how 'explain' questions are marked. The fact that **most particles passed straight through** showed that **most of an atom is empty space**. The fact that **some were deflected** meant that the centre of the atom has a **positive charge** (positive repels positive). The very few that **bounced back** showed that the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a **tiny, dense nucleus**, because only a very concentrated charge could reverse the direction of a fast alpha particle. A spread-out positive charge, as in the plum pudding model, could never do this.

bullets: Nuclear model = **small positive nucleus, electrons orbiting around it**.
The nucleus is about **1/10 000** of the radius of the atom, so most of the atom is empty space.
Total positive charge in the nucleus equals the total negative charge on the electrons, so the atom is **neutral**.
Later experiments showed the positive charge of any nucleus can be divided into **whole-number multiples of a smaller particle, the proton**.
Weakness of the early nuclear model: it did not explain **why the electrons stay in orbit** and do not spiral into the nucleus.
This weakness was fixed by Bohr's idea of fixed energy levels.
core.p: Rutherford's explanation of the results was the **nuclear model**. In this model the atom has a **tiny, positively charged nucleus at the centre**, which contains **most of the mass**, and the **negative electrons** move around the nucleus at a distance, with the rest of the atom empty space. This replaced the plum pudding model and is the basis of the picture of the atom we still use. Rutherford later also provided evidence that the nuclei of different atoms contain different whole numbers of positive particles, which became known as **protons**.

bullets: Bohr's model: electrons orbit in **fixed shells at specific distances** from the nucleus.
Evidence: his calculations **agreed with experimental observations** (for example about the light given off by atoms), so the idea was supported.
Shells are also called **energy levels**; the lowest energy level is the one closest to the nucleus.
This model explains why elements in the same group behave similarly: they have the **same number of outer-shell electrons**.
The model is still used at GCSE because it is simple and explains most of the chemistry we need.
Higher-level science uses further models, which shows that models continue to develop.
core.p: **Niels Bohr** adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that **electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances**, which are called energy levels or **shells**. Electrons cannot exist between these shells. Bohr's **theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations**, which is why the model was accepted. This is the model we use for electronic structure at GCSE, where electrons are placed in shells such as 2,8,1.

bullets: Neutrons are **neutral** (charge 0) and have a **relative mass of 1**.
The nucleus is therefore made of **protons and neutrons**, together called nucleons.
Chadwick's work explained the **missing mass** in the nuclear model.
Neutrons explain **isotopes**: the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
They also help hold the nucleus together (higher level physics, nuclear forces), though that is beyond GCSE chemistry.
Because the neutron has no charge, it is much harder to detect than the electron or proton, which is why it was discovered later.
core.p: The nuclear model could not account for the **mass** of atoms: protons alone were too light to explain atomic masses. **James Chadwick** provided the **experimental evidence for neutrons** in the nucleus, particles with **no charge** and about the same mass as a proton. This came about **20 years after** the nucleus became part of the atomic model. With neutrons included, the model could explain why atoms of the same element can have different masses (isotopes).

bullets: Proton: charge **+1**, mass **1**, found in the **nucleus**.
Neutron: charge **0**, mass **1**, found in the **nucleus**.
Electron: charge **-1**, mass **very small (negligible)**, found in **shells** around the nucleus.
**Number of protons = number of electrons** in a neutral atom.
If an atom gains or loses electrons, it becomes an **ion**: losing electrons gives a positive ion, gaining electrons gives a negative ion.
The number of **protons** never changes in a chemical reaction; it defines the element.
core.h: 10. Subatomic particles: relative charge and relative mass
core.p: You must learn the **relative charge** and **relative mass** of the three subatomic particles. The **proton** has a relative charge of **+1** and a relative mass of **1**. The **neutron** has a relative charge of **0** (neutral) and a relative mass of **1**. The **electron** has a relative charge of **-1** and a **very small** relative mass (about 1/1835 of a proton, so we treat it as negligible). Atoms have **no overall charge** because the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the +1 charges cancel the -1 charges.

bullets: Atom radius **0.1 nm = 1 x 10^-10 m**.
Nucleus radius **1 x 10^-14 m**, which is **1/10 000** of the atom's radius (10^-14 / 10^-10 = 10^-4).
Conversion: **1 nm = 1 x 10^-9 m**, so 0.1 nm = 1 x 10^-10 m.
Because almost all the mass is in the nucleus, the **mass of an atom is approximately the number of protons plus neutrons**.
Standard form is used for these tiny values: be able to read and write numbers such as 1 x 10^-14.
Nuclear diameter comparisons: if an atom were as wide as a football pitch, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea.
core.h: 11. The size and mass of atoms
core.p: Atoms are extremely small, with a **radius of about 0.1 nm** (that is **1 x 10^-10 m**). The **nucleus** is much smaller again: its radius is about **1/10 000** of the radius of the atom, which is about **1 x 10^-14 m**. Even so, the nucleus contains **almost all of the mass** of the atom, because protons and neutrons are about 1835 times heavier than an electron. So most of the **volume** of an atom is empty space occupied by the electrons, while most of the **mass** is in the nucleus.

bullets: **Atomic number = number of protons** (also equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom).
**Mass number = protons + neutrons**.
**Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number**.
Example: sodium, mass number 23, atomic number 11, has **11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons**.
On the periodic table, the **larger number** is the mass number (or relative atomic mass) and the **smaller** is the atomic number (for the usual layout).
For ions, work out electrons by adjusting: Mg2+ has 12 protons but **10 electrons**; Cl- has 17 protons and **18 electrons**.
core.p: The **atomic number** is the **number of protons** in the nucleus, and it is what **defines an element**: all atoms with 6 protons are carbon. The **mass number** is the **total number of protons and neutrons** in the nucleus. The periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number. In nuclear symbols the mass number is written at the top left of the symbol and the atomic number at the bottom left, for example carbon-12 is 12 (top) 6 (bottom) C.

bullets: Isotopes: **same atomic number, different mass number**.
Hydrogen-1 (0 neutrons), hydrogen-2 (1 neutron) and hydrogen-3 (2 neutrons) all have **1 proton**.
Carbon-12: 6 protons, 6 neutrons. Carbon-14: 6 protons, **8 neutrons**.
Chlorine-35: 17 protons, **18 neutrons**. Chlorine-37: 17 protons, **20 neutrons**.
Same electrons mean the **same chemical reactions**; extra neutrons only change the mass.
Some isotopes are **unstable** (radioactive), for example carbon-14, which is covered in the physics atomic structure topic.
core.p: **Isotopes** are different atoms of the **same element** that have the **same number of protons** but a **different number of neutrons**. They therefore have the **same atomic number** but **different mass numbers**. Common examples are hydrogen (hydrogen-1 has 0 neutrons, hydrogen-2 has 1 and hydrogen-3 has 2), carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14, and chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. Isotopes have the **same chemical properties** because chemical reactions depend on the **electrons**, and isotopes have the same number of electrons (same electronic structure). They have different **physical properties** such as mass and density.

bullets: Electronic structure leads to the **group and period** of an element.
Isotopes lead to **relative atomic mass** calculations (next topic).
In Physics: alpha particle = **2 protons + 2 neutrons** (helium nucleus), charge +2.
Radioactive decay changes the **nucleus**, not the electrons, whereas chemical reactions change the **electrons**.
Higher tier: be ready to explain **why** the scattering results contradict plum pudding and support the nuclear model.
Models help us **make predictions**; if a prediction fails, the model is revised.
core.h: 14. Linking to other topics and Higher-tier use
core.p: The atom model underpins almost every other chemistry topic. **Electronic structure** (shells) explains the layout of the **periodic table**, and the number of outer electrons explains **bonding** (ionic, covalent and metallic) and reactivity trends. Isotopes explain why the **relative atomic mass** of an element is rarely a whole number. In **physics**, alpha particles are helium nuclei (2 protons and 2 neutrons), and the alpha scattering experiment is also part of the Physics atomic structure topic, so you should expect to use it in both subjects. At Higher tier, questions often give new data and ask you to **evaluate how it supports or challenges** a model.

exam: Command words: **State** or **name** = 1 mark, one fact (for example 'proton has relative charge +1').
**Describe** the plum pudding model (2 marks): ball of **positive charge** (1) with **negative electrons embedded** in it (1).

**Explain** how the alpha scattering results led to the nuclear model (up to 6 marks): link each observation with its conclusion: **straight through, mostly empty space; deflected, positive nucleus; bounced back, dense nucleus**.
Always write the pattern **observation, therefore conclusion**: marks are for both parts.
Use the word **concentrated**: 'positive charge and mass are concentrated in a small nucleus'.
For particle questions, give **relative charge and relative mass** as numbers (+1, 0, -1; 1, 1, very small).
Neutron calculation (1 mark): **mass number - atomic number**; show it, then give the number.
For **isotope** definitions (2 marks): same number of **protons** (1) different number of **neutrons** (1).
Size questions: use **standard form** and units; 0.1 nm = 1 x 10^-10 m.
When asked 'why did the model change?', mention **new evidence** that the old model could not explain.
Mention **repulsion between like charges** (positive alpha, positive nucleus) for deflection marks.

mistakes.r: Plum pudding has **no nucleus**: positive charge is spread throughout, with negative electrons embedded in it.
mistakes.w: Atoms are solid and the plum pudding has a nucleus.

mistakes.r: **Most passed straight through**; only a **very small number** bounced back.
The nucleus is **positive**, and **positive repels positive**, so alpha particles are deflected.
mistakes.w: The nucleus repels alpha particles because it is negative.

mistakes.r: Electrons have a **very small** relative mass (negligible); protons and neutrons are 1.
Isotopes have the **same number of protons** and **different numbers of neutrons**.
mistakes.w: Isotopes have different numbers of protons.

mistakes.r: **Mass number = protons + neutrons**; atomic number is the number of protons.
mistakes.w: Mass number is the number of protons.

mistakes.r: **Rutherford** (nuclear model); **Bohr** added electrons in **fixed shells at specific distances**.
The nucleus is tiny (about **1/10 000** of the radius) but contains **almost all the mass**.
mistakes.w: The nucleus is big and takes up most of the atom.

mistakes.r: **Thomson** discovered the electron; **Chadwick** provided evidence for the **neutron**.

summary: You must know how the model of the atom developed (Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr, Chadwick) and how new experimental evidence changed each model, plus the structure of the atom: protons, neutrons and electrons, their relative charges and masses, the size of atoms and nuclei, atomic number, mass number and isotopes. It matters because it is the foundation of the whole of chemistry and of physics atomic structure, and it is examined as both recall and 'explain how the evidence led to the model' questions.

A substance made of only one type of atom.

The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A subatomic particle in the nucleus with relative charge +1 and relative mass 1.
A subatomic particle in the nucleus with relative charge 0 and relative mass 1.
A subatomic particle with relative charge -1 and very small relative mass that orbits the nucleus in shells.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons so it has an overall charge.
A fixed region around the nucleus where electrons can be found, at a specific distance from the nucleus.
A unit of length equal to 1 x 10^-9 m.

worked.ans: In the experiment most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, which shows that the atom is mostly empty space. Some alpha particles were deflected because the centre of the atom is positively charged and repels the positive alpha particles. A very small number bounced back, so the positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus. The plum pudding model, with positive charge spread through the atom, could not explain large deflections, so it was replaced by the nuclear model.
worked.q: Describe how the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment led scientists to replace the plum pudding model with the nuclear model. (6 marks)
steps: Plum pudding predicted only small deflections because the positive charge was spread out.
Observation: most alpha particles passed straight through, so most of the atom is empty space.
Observation: some were deflected, so the centre of the atom is positively charged (positive repels positive).
Observation: a very small number bounced back, so the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.
Conclusion: the plum pudding model could not explain this, so the nuclear model replaced it.
